_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Czechia covering Celtic Boii (Bohemia name), Great Moravia (863 Cyril and Methodius), Přemyslid dynasty, Bohemian kingdom (Holy Roman Empire), Charles IV Golden Age (Prague capital of HRE, Charles University 1348), Jan Hus/Hussite Wars (1419-34, proto-Reformation), Habsburg rule (1526-1918), Defenestration of Prague (1618, triggered Thirty Years' War), Battle of White Mountain 1620, Habsburg re-Catholicisation, 1848 revolution, Czechoslovak independence 1918 (Masaryk), Munich Agreement 1938 (betrayal, 'peace for our time'), Nazi Protectorate, Heydrich assassination 1942, Communist coup 1948, Prague Spring 1968 (Soviet invasion), Charter 77, Velvet Revolution 1989 (Havel), Velvet Divorce 1993 (Slovakia split), EU accession 2004.

religion.note: Most irreligious country in Europe (~57% no religion); Habsburg forced re-Catholicisation after 1620 created lasting resentment; Hussite tradition (proto-Protestant); communist atheisation; religion deeply unpopular; cultural Christianity minimal; Jan Hus = national hero (burned at stake 1415 for reform)

country_profile.notes_unique: Prague ('City of a Hundred Spires', UNESCO, most beautiful Central European city); Jan Hus (burned at stake 1415, proto-Reformation 100 years before Luther); Hussite Wars (1419-34, first successful religious revolution in Europe); Defenestration of Prague (1618, triggered Thirty Years' War); Munich Agreement 1938 (Chamberlain betrayed Czechoslovakia to Hitler, 'peace for our time'); Velvet Revolution 1989 (Václav Havel, peaceful end of communism, playwright-president); Velvet Divorce 1993 (peaceful split with Slovakia); most irreligious country in Europe; beer capital of world (highest per capita consumption ~140L/year, pilsner invented in Plzeň 1842); Škoda Auto; Charles University 1348 (oldest in Central Europe); Kafka (Prague German-Jewish writer); Dvořák/Smetana (classical music); not yet in eurozone (by choice); 16 UNESCO World Heritage Sites

910.name: Celtic, Germanic & Early Slavic Bohemia
910.description: The Celtic Boii tribe gave Bohemia its name. Germanic Marcomanni replaced them under Roman-era pressures. Slavic migrations in the 6th century established the population base for future Czech statehood.

sub_clusters.name: Boii & Germanic Period
sub_clusters.description: The Celtic Boii settled Bohemia (giving it its Latin name), followed by the Germanic Marcomanni under Maroboduus (c. 9 BCE–19 CE). The Marcomannic Wars with Rome (166–180 CE) and subsequent Germanic tribal movements shaped the region.

sub_clusters.name: Slavic Settlement & Samo's Empire
sub_clusters.description: Slavic tribes settled Bohemia and Moravia. Samo's tribal union (623–658) — the first recorded Slavic political entity — defeated the Frankish King Dagobert I at Wogastisburg (631/632).
key_events: Samo's Empire — first Slavic political entity (623–658)

920.name: Great Moravia & Přemyslid Dynasty
920.description: Great Moravia was the first major West Slavic state, receiving the mission of Cyril and Methodius (863). The Přemyslid dynasty created the Duchy and later Kingdom of Bohemia, securing the hereditary Bohemian crown within the Holy Roman Empire.

sub_clusters.name: Great Moravia
sub_clusters.description: The Great Moravian Empire under Mojmír I, Rastislav, and Svatopluk. The Byzantine mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius (863) introduced the Glagolitic alphabet and Slavic liturgy. Magyar invasions destroyed the state by 907.
key_events: Mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius to Great Moravia (863)

sub_clusters.name: Přemyslid Duchy & Kingdom of Bohemia
sub_clusters.description: The Přemyslid dynasty united Bohemia: St. Wenceslas (patron saint, murdered 935), the elevation to a kingdom (1198/1212 Golden Bull of Sicily), and Přemysl Ottokar II's brief control of territories from the Baltic to the Adriatic.

920.name: Charles IV & the Luxemburg Golden Age
920.description: The Luxemburg dynasty, especially Charles IV (r. 1346–1378), made Prague the capital of the Holy Roman Empire. Charles University (1348), St. Vitus Cathedral, and the Golden Bull of 1356 marked the zenith of Bohemian power and culture.

sub_clusters.name: Reign of Charles IV
sub_clusters.description: Charles IV made Prague the imperial capital, founded Charles University (1348) — the first university in Central Europe — built the Charles Bridge and New Town, and issued the Golden Bull (1356) codifying imperial electoral procedures.
key_events: Golden Bull of 1356 issued from Prague

sub_clusters.name: Hussite Wars
sub_clusters.description: Jan Hus's reformist preaching, his burning at the Council of Constance (1415), and the subsequent Hussite Wars (1419–1434). The Hussite movement — a proto-Protestant revolution — produced innovative military tactics under Jan Žižka and shaped Czech national identity.
key_events: Jan Hus burned at stake at Council of Constance (July 6, 1415)
Battle of Vítkov Hill — Žižka defeats Crusader army (1420)

930.name: Habsburg Rule & the Thirty Years' War
930.description: The Habsburg acquisition of the Bohemian crown (1526), the growth of Counter-Reformation tensions, the Defenestration of Prague (1618) that ignited the Thirty Years' War, and the post-White Mountain subjugation of Czech autonomy.

sub_clusters.name: Early Habsburg Rule & Counter-Reformation
sub_clusters.description: Ferdinand I's election as King of Bohemia (1526) brought Habsburg rule. Religious tensions between the predominantly Protestant Czech estates and Catholic Habsburgs escalated, despite Rudolf II's Letter of Majesty (1609) granting religious freedom.

sub_clusters.name: Defenestration of Prague & Battle of White Mountain
sub_clusters.description: The Second Defenestration of Prague (May 23, 1618) ignited the Thirty Years' War. The disastrous Czech defeat at White Mountain (1620) led to the execution of 27 rebel leaders, forced re-Catholicisation, germanisation, and the loss of Czech political autonomy for 300 years.
key_events: Defenestration of Prague (May 23, 1618) — triggers Thirty Years' War
Battle of White Mountain (November 8, 1620) — end of Czech independence

sub_clusters.name: Post-White Mountain Era
sub_clusters.description: The Renewed Land Ordinance (1627) eliminated Czech political rights. Forced exile of Protestants (including Jan Amos Comenius), germanisation of the aristocracy, and Baroque cultural transformation of Prague and Bohemian landscapes.

940.name: Czech National Revival & 1848 Revolution
940.description: The Czech National Revival (Národní obrození) revived Czech language and culture from near-extinction. The 1848 Slavic Congress in Prague, industrial growth, and the emergence of competing political programmes (Austroslavism vs. independence) defined this era.

sub_clusters.name: Czech National Revival
sub_clusters.description: Scholars like Josef Dobrovský and Josef Jungmann revived the Czech language from near-extinction. František Palacký's 'History of the Czech Nation' provided a national narrative, and the National Museum (1818) became a symbol of cultural identity.

sub_clusters.name: 1848 Revolution & Industrial Growth
sub_clusters.description: The 1848 Slavic Congress in Prague and Palacký's Austroslavism. Rapid industrialisation made Bohemia the Habsburg Empire's workshop. Czech political parties, the Sokol gymnastic movement, and cultural institutions flourished under late Habsburg rule.

950.name: Czechoslovakia: Independence & Interwar Republic
950.description: Czechoslovakia was founded (October 28, 1918) as a democratic republic under Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk. The interwar republic was Central Europe's only stable democracy but fell victim to the Munich Agreement (1938) and Nazi dismemberment.

sub_clusters.name: Founding of Czechoslovakia
sub_clusters.description: Czech and Slovak émigré action abroad (Masaryk, Beneš, Štefánik), the Czechoslovak Legions in WWI, and the declaration of independence on October 28, 1918 in Prague.

sub_clusters.name: Munich Agreement & Nazi Occupation
sub_clusters.description: The Munich Agreement (September 30, 1938) ceded the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany. The Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia (1939–45), Heydrich's brutal rule, Operation Anthropoid (Heydrich assassination, 1942), and the Lidice massacre.
key_events: Munich Agreement — betrayal by Western allies (September 30, 1938)

950.name: Communist Era & Prague Spring
950.description: The communist coup (February 1948), Stalinist purges (Slánský trial), Dubček's Prague Spring (1968) and its crushing by Warsaw Pact invasion, and the 'normalisation' era of hushed dissent.

sub_clusters.name: Communist Takeover & Stalinist Era
sub_clusters.description: Expulsion of 3 million Sudeten Germans, the communist coup d'état (February 1948), Stalinist purges (Rudolf Slánský trial, 1952), collectivisation, and the construction of a totalitarian state.

sub_clusters.name: Prague Spring & Normalisation
sub_clusters.description: Alexander Dubček's 'socialism with a human face' reforms (Prague Spring, 1968) ended by Warsaw Pact invasion (August 20–21, 1968). Jan Palach's self-immolation (1969), Charter 77 dissident movement (Havel, Patočka), and two decades of 'normalisation'.
key_events: Warsaw Pact invasion crushes Prague Spring (August 20–21, 1968)

960.name: Velvet Revolution & Modern Czechia
960.description: The Velvet Revolution (November 17, 1989) peacefully ended communist rule. The Velvet Divorce (January 1, 1993) separated Czechoslovakia into Czech Republic and Slovakia. EU accession (2004) and continued democratic development.

sub_clusters.name: Velvet Revolution & Transition
sub_clusters.description: The student demonstration of November 17, 1989 ignited the Velvet Revolution. Václav Havel became president. Economic 'shock therapy' under Václav Klaus. The Velvet Divorce (January 1, 1993) peacefully dissolved Czechoslovakia.
key_events: Velvet Divorce — peaceful dissolution of Czechoslovakia (January 1, 1993)

sub_clusters.name: EU Accession & Contemporary Czechia
sub_clusters.description: NATO membership (1999), EU accession (May 1, 2004), economic growth, political debates over euro adoption, the presidency of Miloš Zeman, and Czechia's evolving role in European politics.
